 Food recall readiness: Could you survive a recall tomorrow?
 Agriculture Date posted November 12, 2026 Executive summary
 Being perpetually recall ready takes consistent work and organization. When food packers and shippers are unprepared, recalls can come seemingly out of nowhere, leaving them with a tight timeframe to react and carry out complex emergency protocols. If your food packing or shipping business works across disparate systems, spreadsheets and paper records, it’s even harder to find the information you need, analyze it, act on it and share it to meet expectations in the tight timeframe of a recall event. 
 If you’re unsure if your team is prepared to handle a recall, implementing a food safety software solution like TELUS Food Safety and Quality is a wise investment. It’s designed to make the process much more manageable. It enables faster access to information, enhanced product visibility, a more coordinated recall response, confident decision making and minimal admin work. 
 Key takeaways:
 Food recall severity and spread reached disastrous levels in the US in 2026 putting food packers and shippers in the hot seat
 Recalls can catch food packing and shipping businesses off guard, leaving you with little to no time to find critical information, analyze it and share it in an organized way with impacted parties
 Handling a recall can be particularly challenging when your business is dealing with disparate systems, spreadsheets and paper records
 Modern food safety software can isolate impacted product lots in seconds, protecting both your bottom line and brand reputation
 Recalls are a worrying issue in the US
 In 2026, recall headlines have dominated consumer news. While total recall frequency remained steady , the sheer volume of affected food and outbreak severity reached multi-year highs. Fiscal 2026 has had 500 US recalls , and this year’s Cyclospora infections surged past 18,000 cases . Staple foods like lettuce, blueberries and eggs were affected, leaving consumers unsure of what’s safe to eat.
 This loss of consumer confidence has put food packers and shippers in the hot seat. Recalls are tough enough when the public isn’t already agitated. In the event of a recall, packers and shippers have to immediately:
 Stop distributing the impacted product
 Identify, isolate and trace affected lots 
 Notify customers and regulators
 Submit a Reportable Food Registry (RFR) filing to the FDA within 24 hours  
 Provide instructions for return or disposal
 Carry out recall procedures and document all actions
 Verify the product has been removed and properly reprocess, divert or destroy it
 Every packer knows the drill when disaster strikes, but that doesn’t make it any less of a scramble when a recall happens – especially when the company works across disparate systems, spreadsheets and paper records. The call comes in, the clock starts ticking and an unprepared business easily gets bogged down by time-consuming and error-prone manual data extraction and reconciliation efforts. But if a company puts the right tools in place before disaster strikes, a recall doesn’t have to be a race.
 How to tell if you could survive a recall
 Recalls aren’t inevitable, but they’re also not out of the realm of possibility. Is your team prepared for one? If you want to assess your recall readiness, start by asking your team these questions:
 How quickly could we trace affected products?
 Could we access critical documentation immediately?
 Could we comply with the FDA’s 24-hour deadline to submit a Reportable Food Registry filing?
 How fast could we identify affected suppliers?
 Does everyone in our team know what to do in a recall?
 When did we run our last test for our recall protocol?
 If you run through these tough questions with your team and get disconcerting answers, you may not be ready for a recall.

 Explore the solution Why navigating recalls will only get harder
 Without the right system in place, handling a recall today could be a logistical nightmare for your business. The pressure is only going to compound in 2028 when FSMA section 204 , the Food Traceability Rule, comes into effect, adding even more to-do items to your recall protocol. To comply, food packers and shippers will need to :
 Record Critical Tracking Events ( CTEs ) which are points in the food supply chain where traceability data must be collected
 Capture Key Data Elements ( KDEs ) which record details related to a product's CTEs
 Maintain a traceability plan for foods on the Food Traceability List ( FTL )
 Maintain records and send them in an electronic sortable spreadsheet to the US Food and Drug Administration (the FDA) within 24 hours of a request
 How to boost your recall readiness today
 The right food safety software solution can help prepare your business for the hefty demands of a recall today – and ensure you’re ready to comply with FSMA 204’s requirements tomorrow . Solutions like TELUS Food Safety and Quality can empower your business with:
 Faster access to information
 Better product visibility
 A more coordinated recall response
 Confident decision making
 Reduced admin work
 A tale of two produce packers: 48 hours under pressure
 To show how a prepared business compares to an unprepared one during a crisis, we tracked two produce packers over the exact same 48-hour window.
 Both receive an urgent FDA notice linking their romaine lettuce shipments to an E. coli outbreak. Both face identical regulatory deadlines and compliance demands. They both have the same goal and deadline, but their stories couldn’t be more different.

 Frequently asked questions
 What actually happens in the first 48 hours after a recall is triggered?
 In the 48 hour timeframe the impacted businesses must immediately stop distributing the impacted product, and follow several steps. These include:
 Identify, isolate and trace affected lots
 Notify customers and regulators 
 Comply with the FDA’s 24-hour deadline to submit a Reportable Food Registry filing
 Provide instructions for return or disposal
 Carry out recall procedures and document all actions
 Verify the product has been removed and properly reprocess, divert or destroy it
 Report their investigation and actions to the FDA
 This can take much longer than 48 hours if the business is ill prepared for a recall, and failure to comply may lead the business to quarantine and destroy more products than necessary at great expense.
 How can we test if our team is truly prepared for a food recall?
 Run an unannounced mock recall. Select a random historical lot and attempt to trace its origin, processing steps, customer destinations and associated test logs within a strict 24-hour window.
 What's the difference between a recall and a product withdrawal, and does it matter for my response plan?
 A product recall involves removing a food product from the market due to a health or safety risk (such as the presence of allergens or physical contamination) or because it violates legal standards. Recalls require you to quickly notify regulatory agencies like the FDA, submit a Reportable Food Registry filing within 24 hours and issue public warnings and corrective action reports. 
 Withdrawals address minor quality or packing issues before the product has reached consumers, and do not require public alerts or regulatory oversight.
 Recalls vs withdrawals warrant distinct reaction times, communication protocols and reporting requirements. A withdrawal triggers targeted holds with logistics partners and internal analysis to root out issues with products, while a recall relies on crisis teams who notify authorities, draft public notices, and execute full product tracking to ensure the safe removal of contaminated products from the food supply. 
 Who needs to be notified first when a potential recall issue is discovered internally?
 In the event of a potential recall, the first person to notify is your facility’s Internal Recall Coordinator or Quality Assurance (QA) Lead. That individual will halt affected packaging lines and freeze distribution of potentially contaminated inventory. Your company’s recall team will then assess the health hazard to confirm whether a recall is necessary. If a safety issue is confirmed, then it’s time to notify the FDA within their required timelines, such as within 24 hours, and submit a Reported Food Registry filing. After that it’s time to contact supply chain partners , affected customers and the general public if the affected food has been sold.
